items.question: How do you judge whether an investment in AI model training is successful?
items.object: Evaluating AI model investment through product outcomes
items.answer: I think the purpose of those model is to serve product. The model by itself doesn't have any meaning. If model training doesn't move the needle for product, it's not meaningful. It's not useful. Product AB testing is the ultimate judge whether your model investment is paying off or not, is successful or not. So actually the fast iteration experimentation loop has both training and inference combined together to declare a victory.
quotes: The purpose of those model is to serve product. The model by itself doesn't have any meaning. If model training doesn't move the needle for product, it's not meaningful. It's not useful. Product AB testing is the ultimate judge whether your model investment is paying off or not, is successful or not. So actually the fast iteration experimentation loop has both training and inference combined together to declare a victory.

rubrics.text: The response states that AI model-training investment is meaningful only if it improves product outcomes.
The response identifies product A/B testing as the ultimate judge of whether AI model-training investment is successful.
The response describes training and inference as parts of a single rapid experimentation loop for evaluating model improvements.

items.question: How did your experience moving between research and building systems shape your motivation to create Fireworks AI?
items.object: Lin Qiao’s motivation to create Fireworks AI
items.answer: It's kind of full circle in my career: to do research, go build systems, and come back to system research, code design space. So that has been a very fun journey, and the visibility we got from driving the AI work at Meta really gave us confidence this is going to be a huge industrial transformation. And that's our motivation to create Fireworks, to help all developers in the industry using AI in a very easy way.

items.question: How do you see Fireworks’ role in helping developers focus on building generative AI applications?
items.object: Fireworks’ role in generative AI application development
items.answer: Fireworks is our gen AI SaaS platform where you do not need to set up anything. Do not need to worry about how many GPUs you need to kind of deploy to run your application, where is the location, how to manage reliability, cost, performance optimization, none of those. You just onboard to Fireworks and integrate with your product, and boom, it will automate itself. It will help you save cost and scale quickly to millions of developers or billions of consumers. We manage all the production operation complexity and let you focus on application product development.

items.question: How do you see AI developers’ needs changing as they move from experimentation to scaling in production?
items.object: AI developers’ needs during experimentation and production scaling
items.answer: We really see the developer needs are not uniform. It at least broke into two phases, if not more. In the most simplistic way, the first bulk of developer work is experimentation, and that's where you want fast iteration, simple integration, lots of control, and validate your hypothesis, what can work, what may not work, and fail fast. So that's kind of the speed of iteration is the most important; productivity is most important. Once you find product-market fit, maybe one out of 10 ideas survive for you to scale into production, then it's a complete different set of problem to tackle. That's where you need to worry about cost efficiency to have viable business, to worry about latency to bring the interactive experience of consumer-facing, developer-facing product live. You need to worry about quality to the next level—how does model quality really feed into the product needs? So all of that becomes a different set of concern. So we have seen issues only focus on one versus the other, meaning only the fast iteration or only the high efficiency scaling.
quotes: So we really see the developer needs are not uniform. It at least broke into two phases, if not more.

items.question: Why do you think a developer platform needs to support smooth transitions across the entire product development life cycle?
items.object: End-to-end developer platform design
items.answer: If this conversion takes a month, they're like, “Oh my God, we are just doing nothing but waiting for this to happen, and this is not working for me.” So the product team is heavily depending on the fast iteration with their users to understand whether the new product design is landing well with the customer or not, because there are a lot of hypothesis: what power feature become popular, will it drive user engagement, drive time span, drive a lot of metrics? But it's not validated until they see the AB testing results. So that's the nature of fast iteration. There's a fast iteration with the end user also that need to happen; that cannot be slowed down. So that's where this whole SaaS platform design cannot just be one-sided, kind of any one phase of the development life cycle, of the production life cycle. It need to be end to end, very smooth transition. So that I would say that's going to be the biggest lesson learned, and that's why in Fireworks we always think about ourself as we're building towards the end to end developer platform.

items.question: Why do you see inference as the foundation of Fireworks' end-to-end developer platform?
items.object: Inference as the foundation of Fireworks' end-to-end developer platform
items.answer: We start with inference because inference is the foundation of this end to end. Inference is foundation because if you think about post-training, we build on top of open models. One thing I want to clarify is Fireworks, we do not do pre-training, we do not build foundation models, because today the open model quality is really good, especially this month is the gift showering—all high quality models. We can talk a lot more; I'm very passionate about that. In the open world model world a lot of people are doing tuning and customization. And part of the popular tuning technology is called RFT, or reinforcement fine-tuning. If you take a deeper look at reinforcement fine-tuning, it is training; it is inference for rollouts. And actually even for tuning it has a lot of inference dependency, and obviously after tuning you need to deploy to small scale AB testing—that's inference—and then scale to full production traffic, that's also inference. So that's why inference is a foundation of this end to end. We started with inference at the beginning, and then we added supervised fine-tuning. We added reinforcement fine-tuning, all different kind of tuning customization technology built on top of inference.

items.question: How do you think inference abstractions should serve developers as they move from validating product-market fit to operating at scale?
items.object: Developer abstractions for inference at different stages of product development
items.answer: So I will start on inference. There are people who just want to validate if gen AI is the right tool to solve their product problem or not. So that's why we choose OpenAI-compatible API. Obviously everyone choose OpenAI-compatible. It's just kind of easier to speak the same language. But then when they graduate from product market fit validation phase to scale, then there are a lot of customization for inference itself to be high speed, cost efficient, and also quality need to be really good. So we call a three-dimensional optimization. We build a 3D optimizer to drive the customization for our developers without them understanding deeply how to customize their inference deployment to satisfy their needs. So that is a layer of abstraction we created, very similar to a concept of query optimizer for databases.

items.question: How do you approach optimizing AI inference across the many system configurations while meeting a product team's quality and performance requirements?
items.object: Systematic optimization of AI inference
items.answer: So there are many dimensions. For example, for inference we do fully disaggregated inference. That means we chop the model execution by the system bottleneck. Some part of model execution is fully bottlenecked by compute. Some are fully bottlenecked by memory access. Some are fully bottlenecked by networking. And we disaggregate them and scale them independently. And then how to scale them really depends on the workflow pattern and the performance characteristics that the product team is looking at from the product requirement. So that is one way to look at it. On top of that there are various different numerics you can apply in terms of precision. When you apply precision, this technique is called quantization. You can quantize so many different things, and there's a lot of options in that space. Not just you can pick different precision; you can also quantize weights, quantize activation, quantize communication. You can quantize many. But at the same time when you quantize by default your quality goes down. Sometimes if you quantize naively your quality goes down by a lot. A lot of product use case cannot have that trade-off. They cannot trade off quality with speed, quality with cost. They want to preserve the quality, do not degrade, and then improve the other two. So then we have a technique, and then we have a way to preserve the quality while doing this optimization. We also have different kernels implemented for optimizing for different context length, the long context, shorter context, and for generation speed there are different options we can pick and choose from there. Obviously we also have optimization for different hardware back ends, because different hardware have their unique strength we can leverage. So that's where the search space is very big, and you cannot manually try all these combinations; it need to be done in a systematic way.

items.question: How do you think about when to optimize AI inference—during runtime or before deployment?
items.object: Runtime and predeployment optimization for AI inference
items.answer: It's a combination. Some of the optimization we can do during runtime. Some of optimization we're going to push before we deploy. So it's like how compiler work—there's JIT, there's AOT. We're doing a combination of both.
quotes: It's a combination. Some of the optimization we can do during runtime. Some of optimization we're going to push before we deploy.
Yeah, so it's like how compiler work—there's JIT, there's AOT. We're doing a combination of both.

rubrics.text: The response likens combining runtime and predeployment inference optimization to combining just-in-time (JIT) and ahead-of-time (AOT) compilation.

items.question: Why do you think developers want their AI products to be model agnostic?
items.object: Model agnosticism in AI product development
items.answer: Often time we see a desire from many developer: they want to be model agnostic. When they build a product they don't want to get bundled with a model because this space moves so fast. Almost every week there's a new model being announced, whether it's closed or open. Some model is breaking some record somewhere. And there's a huge amount of desire to be model agnostic.
quotes: That's a very interesting topic, because often time we see a desire from many developer: they want to be model agnostic. Some model is breaking some record somewhere. And there's a huge amount of desire to be model agnostic.

rubrics.text: The response explains that rapid advances in AI models motivate developers to avoid tying their products to a single model.

items.question: How do you see a product's stage of development shaping its choice of AI model?
items.object: Model selection over the product development life cycle
items.answer: The interesting observation is it also depends on the product life cycle itself. In the early stage of product development, when people are not sure which part of this product feature can be hardened yet, they typically would pick a powerful model to begin with, just kind of ensure the best quality. Over time they got a lot of user feedback. There are AB testing, there are metrics to monitor each part of feature, how people's reaction look like and how they kind of continue to polish it and tune it to a point it start to emerge: those features win to harden. Typically those features have a narrower problem definition, and that's where they start specialize and customize. We see a clear and continuous transition. It's never done one shot, from “I have a new product idea, I want to try it on the most powerful model” to “now I know exactly what I want to field and I'm going to narrow down and use a special customized model.” The customization process can be: I pick another smaller specialized model from off the shelf, or now I have bootstrap my product, I have a lot of data from production to tune the model specific for my application.

items.question: Why do you think overfitting a model to a particular application can be desirable?
items.object: Application-specific model overfitting and the product feedback cycle
items.answer: There's a lot of power to unleash from there because no one has that data. Not the Frontier Labs, nobody. And with that data, you can overfit your model into your application. That's what you want to do. Actually, in this case, overfitting is good. And therefore the model is designed for your product, make your product better, and your better product draw more user engagement. You collect more data, make the model better, better product and so on. So this is a virtual cycle we start to build. We see a lot of success for early pilots being able to master that virtual cycle, and they emerge as leaders in current gen app space.

items.question: What makes standardizing reinforcement fine-tuning tools difficult in your view?
items.object: Standardizing reinforcement fine-tuning tools and reward evaluators
items.answer: What we are convinced to do and to offer value to this community is to make those tools accessible to everyone. It should be easy, it should be standardized. But when it comes to standardization, it's a messy, very messy place. Let's talk about one technique that's getting very popular and also we offer on our platform: reinforcement fine-tuning, RFT. The most critical part of RFT is to write an evaluator that takes a model output, gives a score. That score is called reward. You give a very big positive score, that means you really want the model doing a great job; you can nudge it to the right direction. A big negative score means the model is really bad, the result is BS, and you want to strongly discourage it going that direction. A lot of reward you can write in code and can be executed in isolation. But a lot of time you cannot write it in code. You have to call into an application-specific internal API to extract knowledge and information that is deeply coupled with the product. Because a lot of time those kinds of score generation or reward generation depend on internal state.

items.question: How do you view the prospect of models continuously training on user feedback within live applications?
items.object: Continuous online model training from user feedback
items.answer: I'm very bullish on that direction. I think we should have that. The biggest challenge today is, in order for us to have that, people need to write what is the expectation for the model to grow into that expectation. It's like when we want to test our code, we need to first write unit test. Unit test is basically I expect this piece of code to behave this way, and I'm going to test it. Then I know if the code is doing the good job or not. So that's kind of similar to reward.

items.question: Why do you see clear model evaluation criteria as the starting point for automatically closing the loop between AI training and inference?
items.object: Clear model evaluation criteria as the foundation for automatically closing the loop between AI training and inference
items.answer: I don't think we can kick the can down the road, because without a good evaluation mechanism defined, many things are harder. All the things we talk about is going to be harder. For example, earlier we talked about people do want to be model agnostic, but without the evaluation criteria defined, when they switch models they don't have a way to measure: should they switch or not? Anything is going to regress or is going to improve? I don't want to be surprised. So evaluation is also needed for RFT, because you need to have a way to tell the model, in comparison to expectation, is it doing good job or not. So before we do anything, I think one of the common practice that is spreading to the industry is to have developers write evals. That's a starting point. Without that, a lot of things they do is like shooting in the dark. They'll start vibe checking, but vibe checking is not reliable, it's not consistent, it's not repeatable, it's not systematic. I think that before anything, the future I'm very bullish about, to close the loop automatically, the first thing is to enable everyone to write clear evaluation criteria. I think that's a transition the industry is moving towards. Many app developer are very familiar with product analytics stack: I can start to trace this and build data pipeline to generate product metrics, and I know how to do AB testing, and then I know how to look at the result and make decisions and do a lot of product-level experimentation. But how do I write evaluation for this model is a new skill I need to learn. I haven't worked on that before, but we see people are picking that best practice faster than ever. So this is an exciting moment, but also at the same time it's a starting point of doing this automatic closed loop thing.

items.question: How do you think AI training developer tools should balance low-level control with higher-level abstractions?
items.object: Layered abstractions in AI training developer tools
items.answer: We are aiming at a broad set of developers. But in the adoption curve of a new technology it almost always start with power users. People are self-learners. They can go really deep and pick it up and adopt it. So, for the power user, the pattern is they want to control everything. They want to tweak a lot of knobs without being blocked out of optionalities. If you give them a higher level abstraction, they will be so frustrated and they will not like it. Instead, they want to go as low as possible. So the system design is just build building blocks and expose knobs for them to tune. But then when you want to reach a broader set of audience, lots of people don't want to tune low-level knobs. They want to focus on developing product and just have simple integration and things should just work. By things just work it means out of box it has preconfigured setup that can bring you to 80%. May not be 100% or like 90%, but 80% to begin with is good enough. So that's a high-level, simpler abstraction for a broad set audience. We have tested this hypothesis many times and this setup is the best to cover both ends. The good news is the higher-level abstraction can build on top of the lower-level abstraction. It's a staggered system, and in that sense it's not wasted effort to build lower level. I believe in this design, and we also think what's happening during training space is also following that pattern.

They want to focus on developing product and just have simple integration and things should just work. By things just work it means out of box it has preconfigured setup that can bring you to 80%. May not be 100% or like 90%, but 80% to begin with is good enough. So that's a high-level, simpler abstraction for a broad set audience.

We have tested this hypothesis many times and this setup is the best to cover both ends. The good news is the higher-level abstraction can build on top of the lower-level abstraction. It's a staggered system, and in that sense it's not wasted effort to build lower level. I believe in this design, and we also think what's happening during training space is also following that pattern.

items.question: How do you think a reinforcement fine-tuning interface should make low-level controls accessible to developers with different levels of experience?
items.object: The developer experience for reinforcement fine-tuning
items.answer: For example, in reinforcement fine-tuning, there are many parameters, just kind of the tuning parameters, but also some for the initial setup. We have a web app; you can write your evaluators, the code of reward function, and then you can test with your initial small data set. That's easy, that's simple. Once you are confident with the direction of the evaluator or reward function, then you start to upload a real data set and start to kick off a training job. The training job has a lot of parameters that you can set, but we have the default ones. You don't have to worry, just kick off a training job and go with our default ones. Then we also have default parameters, metrics you can look into, but you can add your own metrics. Next-level researchers want to add a lot more details, because the metrics can be overwhelming. If it's not actionable, if you look at those charts and you don't know what do I do—it's going up or going down, even if I understand it, I don't know what's the action to change it—then it's overwhelming. It's useless. So that's what I mean is the first mile for a broader set of audience. We designed that way, but people can click open the parameters; they can set their own thing if they want. Hopefully that will bring a wide range of experience to a broader set of audience that way.

items.question: How do you think generative AI is changing the product development philosophy for application builders?
items.object: Generative AI product development and the gap between frontier-model data and application data
items.answer: If we take a big step back, in this new wave of gen AI the product development philosophy is also changing. Many people we've seen building a great product, having a huge amount of adoption over a small amount of time, do not think of the model as a commodity or just a utility you plug in as is. They think about the model as a critical part, critical assets of their product. They are actively bridging a very interesting gap. The interesting gap is the data they collect from application cannot be seen or accessible to the frontier labs developing models. You can think there are two parallel threads of data distribution that's happening. One is the frontier labs, whether it's closed or open source model providers. They have a dedicated research and data team to curate data based on some assumptions of how application is going to use this model. They curate data based on some data distribution, and that's where the end result, the model quality, is going to focus on. In a different company the application product developers are building new user experiences, and that produces another set of data distribution. By design these two are completely different from each other; they diverge from each other. They solve different problems, and they're different entities. So the mismatch between these two data distributions is going to result in worse quality, worse latency, worse cost. You leave a lot on the table. We firmly believe there's a huge void in that space to standardize, to bring more tools and the platform to close the loop, because we believe a large portion of data actually is not on internet. A large portion of data lives with application itself. If you do not leverage that, there's just a lot of—you know, data is the mode and data flying well is the mode, and you just leave that on the table. Whoever can leverage that quickly and in the best way, they are going to emerge as winner faster. So that's part we want to standardize and productionize soon.

items.question: Why do you see data quality as the essential source of differentiation between AI models?
items.object: Data quality as the source of AI model differentiation
items.answer: If we take a big step back, the model quality is essentially data. It's data quality, that's pretty much clear, because I don't believe any lab has perpetual secret sauce in terms of, for the same amount of data, they just can make the model better in a meaningful way, and nowhere else knows how to make do. But as you can see, people move around a lot and they bring the knowledge with them and spread the knowledge across the industry. So then essentially it's about data, and the public data on internet has been exhausted. There are many data labeling companies; they're pretty much providing services to all the labs, and in that sense there's not much differentiation.

items.question: Where do you see a unique competitive advantage in AI data when multiple labs can use the same data-labeling services?
items.object: Application-specific data as a competitive asset
items.answer: There are 10 different data labeling companies, so no one has the unique advantage. This is such a high potential space and a lot of investment comes in, and that means a lot of companies are going to work in a similar space to bring supporting services to the broader audience. If all the labs essentially have access to the same amount of data, then the only difference is in the app space: they cannot have access to this application-specific data. I think the app space of data is going to be verticalized because that is an asset, that is a unique competitive edge, and no one will share outside. Then the next-level question is how do you leverage that and turn that into your own model advantage?

items.question: Why are you betting your company on customization based on open models?
items.object: Customization based on open models
items.answer: An open model is much easier to tune because there are a lot of tools building around open models in the community that moves really fast. I have many stories, and that's why I believe in the open source community. Even for the originator of some open model provider, open source project provider, at some point they flip to closed source; they build, they close it up for internal use. Their cases again and again show the open source project moves much faster than closed source. I've seen that at Meta, so Meta is a really open-source-friendly company, especially on the infrastructure level. They open source a project and there's too much maintenance to keep the community up, and they decide, “Internal demand is huge on that project, let's just close it up and focus on internal need.” It turns out the open source side moves much faster because the sheer amount of resource is much bigger, no matter what. So that's where I believe, and we're betting as a company in that direction, to bet on customization based on open models, because the whole entire community is working around that and we want to provide easy access of the SaaS platform for people to deploy without considering or solving any of the infrastructure problems. So that's our deepest value proposition, and now we're not just an inference provider but also deeply in the customization, tuning side.

items.question: Why do you find the convergence between open and closed AI models exciting for customization?
items.object: Convergence between open and closed AI models and its implications for customization
items.answer: The model more or less is going to converge on some dimensions. The open model is going to be catching up with closed model closer and closer, which is happening today. All the model provider, when they announce their model, they will show benchmarks against the best. It doesn't matter if it's closed model or open model; they all compare themselves against the best across industry and they will say, “Hey, we beat the best in those metrics.” That makes me excited, because before the open model only compared with open models and compare with each other. Now they're declaring victory against the closed models, and it happens more and more often these days. So that's a sign that the models are all converging. Under the assumption models are all convergent, then the customization based on open model becomes much more interesting, because you do not need to customize to catch up with closed model. You can customize to beat the closed models. That's a very interesting shift of the dynamics happening across industry right now, and our belief in that direction never changes. We have been betting on the open model war to converge with closed model very closely.

items.question: How do you think about the work required to support newly released models on your platform?
items.object: Supporting newly released models on an inference platform
items.answer: We always aim at supporting those models from day zero. Whenever they launch, it's available on platform so people can evaluate those models quickly, and then we will roll out the surrounding functionality. For example, a lot of those models are really good at tool calls, and we need to enable tool call to make it work well with our service APIs, with on-demand, some kind of reserved throughput setup, and all this. The context window length is becoming bigger, and we need to enable that properly. Obviously, a longer context window just means more pressure on processing those tokens, generating those tokens, and so on. So a lot of next-level optimization; some models come with new model components that we need to next-level optimize for.

I think this community is very active right now, and really looking forward to more state-of-the-art model launches from open model world.

items.question: How do you approach getting a new model ready to launch on your inference platform?
items.object: The engineering workflow for supporting a new model in an inference engine
items.answer: Our inference engine has a lot of building blocks. First of all we need to pick the right building blocks to assemble for a particular model. Then this 3D optimization has many options, and we need to go through this search space and find an option we like, and then run a lot of quality testing to make sure the quality is correct. When we assemble those pieces, we need to make sure there are not numeric errors that lead to accuracy issues, so more like focus on quality correctness at the beginning. Then there are other functionalities. There is constraint generation correctness. There are many add-on capabilities on top of the raw inference. There's tool calls. There is LoRA adapter. There are many other things we also need to make sure work well with that particular model. Then we launch it and start to do continuous optimization. So that's the typical workflow.

items.question: Why do you see making generative AI customization accessible to all developers as the most exciting next phase?
items.object: Making generative AI customization accessible to all developers
items.answer: I do think making customization accessible to all developers is the most exciting trend, and we're fully committed to make that happen. But I think it's not just us; the bigger community is actively thinking about that. There are many players covering different sets, different part of this journey for customization, actively building tools. I do think that's the next phase of heavy development and adoption is going to happen there. People will not just be satisfied with using off-the-shelf APIs. They want to actually fully leverage the production data, curated and in a closed loop. This is a different loop, but the mentality on my side is similar to before, of closing the product analytics loop. This is a new loop that they're going to close, and therefore they have their own data to have their own model and build their own leading position in a heavily competitive space of application development. So we would love to see those app developer continue to be very successful in leveraging their own data.
